name: Dynamic tariff bundled with devices or smart metering
summary: A supplier sells hourly-priced electricity and bundles it with devices (smart meter bridge, wallbox, heat pump or battery installation) and an app that shifts consumption to cheap hours.
how_it_makes_money: Supply margin and service fees from the electricity contract; devices and installation are sold or discounted to win customers who can use dynamic prices.

hardware: Smart meter or meter reader bridge
Wallbox, battery or heat pump (optional bundle)
financing: Device subsidies funded from expected supply margin
channel: Direct digital sales, comparison, partner referrals

stakeholder_value.customer: Lower cost if load is shifted

what_must_be_true: Customers have a smart meter or a bridge device
Customers own loads they can shift
Supplier can price and hedge dynamic supply
Customer acquisition cost stays below lifetime margin

risks_failure_causes.text: Smart meter coverage gates how many customers can take the tariff
Customers carry month-to-month price variability, which can put off households
Customers without working connectivity or meters cannot be served

cases.note: Offers a bridge reader (Tibber Pulse) for digital meters so customers can use dynamic prices without a smart meter, and offers wallbox purchase with installation.
Some especially cheap smart tariffs are bundled with installation of a heat pump, battery or solar. Octopus, Tibber and Rabot started a smart meter initiative in Germany.

sources.title: RESET: Consume energy when it's cheap and green with dynamic electricity tariffs

Ostrom: Smart Meter Initiative

name: Energy performance contract: guaranteed savings
summary: An energy service company implements efficiency measures and guarantees a minimum level of savings. If savings fall short it compensates the customer; the customer usually finances the project.
how_it_makes_money: Fee for project delivery and service, tied to the guaranteed savings level; savings above the guarantee may be split with the customer.

hardware: Efficiency measures installed in the building or plant
software: Monitoring and measurement and verification tooling
sites_assets: Customer buildings or facilities, often public
partners: Banks or financiers lending to the customer
financing: Usually customer-financed, with the ESCO guarantee supporting the loan
channel: Tenders and direct sales to public and commercial owners

stakeholder_value.customer: Guaranteed bill reduction with performance risk moved to the ESCO
stakeholder_value.provider: Project and service revenue, upside above the guarantee

what_must_be_true: Baseline and verification method are agreed up front
Real savings reliably exceed the guarantee with a safety buffer
Customer is creditworthy and can finance the project
Procurement rules allow performance-based contracts

risks_failure_causes.text: Disagreement on baseline adjustments or measured savings
ESCO must compensate the customer if savings fall below the guarantee
Public agencies may lack procurement rules or understanding for performance contracting

cases.note: Guaranteed savings is reported as the most common EPC type in Europe and heavily used in North America, Africa, the Middle East and Australia.

sources.title: IEA: Energy performance contract models
JRC Green Best Practice: energy performance contracting

name: Energy performance contract: shared savings
summary: The ESCO finances and delivers the project and is repaid with an agreed share of the energy savings over a fixed period. The ESCO carries financing and performance risk.
how_it_makes_money: Pre-agreed percentage of verified savings for a fixed number of years; a larger share goes to the ESCO because of the up-front investment.

hardware: Efficiency measures installed by the ESCO
regulation: Accounting treatment of the contract (on or off balance sheet)
financing: ESCO funds the project from its own funds or loans and carries credit risk

stakeholder_value.customer: No up-front investment; pays out of savings
stakeholder_value.provider: Share of savings over the term
stakeholder_value.other: Lenders to the ESCO bear credit risk

what_must_be_true: Savings can be measured credibly and customers do not contest them
Savings are large enough to repay the ESCO's investment within the term
ESCO has access to financing
Customer accepts a larger savings share going to the provider

risks_failure_causes.text: Owners have an incentive to challenge measured savings to reduce payments
ESCO-financed projects are more expensive and less capital efficient for the provider
More complex contracts than guaranteed savings; accounting treatment issues

cases.note: Shared savings is used in over 75 percent of contracts according to the IEA.
Guaranteed savings is more common in Europe than shared savings. A 2013 US state document notes that shared savings is rarely favored by owners.

sources.title: IEA: Energy performance contract models
Hawaii State Energy Office: Pros and cons of guaranteed vs shared energy savings (2013)

name: EV charge point operation (three operating models)
summary: Operators run charging hardware under three main models: network operator (sell hardware, earn network fees), owner-operator (own sites, set prices) and charging-as-a-service (turnkey solution for a subscription fee).
how_it_makes_money: Margin on energy sold, subscription or network fees, or hardware and service fees, depending on model; profitability depends on utilisation because fixed costs are high.

stakeholder_value.partner: Site host revenue share or turnkey service

what_must_be_true: Utilisation is high enough to cover fixed costs
Grid capacity is available at the site
Customers return and prices stay competitive

risks_failure_causes.text: A 2021 BCG analysis found most business models unprofitable because of low charger utilisation
Revenue depends on energy sold while fixed costs do not shrink, so payback is long
Grid capacity increasingly constrains where operators can build

cases.note: Sells hardware to site hosts and earns network fees; the host sets the price.
Owns infrastructure, sets prices, relies on driver subscription fees and high utilisation.
Turnkey solution for site owners for a recurring subscription fee.
German startup with battery-backed fast chargers, mostly at retail sites, filed for insolvency in August 2024.

name: Heat contracting (Wärmelieferung) in rented buildings
summary: A landlord outsources heat generation and supply to a contractor who installs, runs and maintains the heating plant; the cost is passed on to tenants through heating bills.
how_it_makes_money: The contractor sells heat at a price formula agreed with the landlord. Capital costs and profit are included in the price that tenants end up paying.

hardware: Heating plant, often continuing to run the existing gas boiler

stakeholder_value.customer: Landlord: no investment and less risk; tenants: not clearly better off

what_must_be_true: Price formulas hold up legally
Cost neutrality for tenants can be shown or avoided
Landlord-contractor relationships stay acceptable to regulators and tenants

risks_failure_causes.text: Journalists and tenant groups report that price formulas are factually wrong, ineffective or contested and tenant costs rise
The German Tenants' Association demands binding rules and a price cap for heat supply contracts in rented buildings
Contractors that are subsidiaries of the landlord weaken the efficiency incentive; often the old gas boiler simply keeps running

cases.note: Around four million apartments are supplied under contracting contracts according to industry figures, but how many benefit financially is questioned. Consumer groups estimate at least hundreds of thousands of tenants pay too much.

sources.title: Utopia: Hunderttausende Mieter zahlen zu hohe Heizkosten (Correctiv research)

name: Heat pump rental or subscription
summary: The provider owns or finances the heat pump and the customer pays a fixed monthly fee instead of buying it. Variants range from pure rental to subscription with maintenance.
how_it_makes_money: Monthly fee over a multi-year term that recovers equipment, installation and financing cost plus margin; service and maintenance may be bundled.

sites_assets: Customer buildings (homes, or rented commercial and public buildings)
regulation: Subsidy rules (differ for rented vs owned equipment)
financing: Provider or investor funds the equipment up front and recovers it through fees
data: Operating data to support service and performance claims

stakeholder_value.customer: No upfront cost, predictable monthly payment
stakeholder_value.other: Landlord-tenant split incentive can be resolved by a third-party owner (HP SUBSCRIBE rationale)

what_must_be_true: Provider can fund equipment cheaply enough that the fee over the term stays acceptable to customers
Customers accept a long contract
Fee is not seen as much more expensive than buying
Service costs over the term are controlled

risks_failure_causes.text: Competitors argue customers pay many times the equipment value over a long rental term; this perception can undermine uptake (claim by a competitor, not independent evidence)
Cost of capital and long payback on provider-owned equipment can make the fee uncompetitive against instalment purchase
Customers dislike being locked into long-term contracts

cases.note: In 2023 a rental at a fixed monthly price was announced with a target of about 10,000 installs. In 2025 Thermondo raised EUR 50M for an instalment purchase model where customers own the heat pump from the start. The sources do not state why or whether rental stopped.
Positions an instalment purchase (5.99 percent financing) against rental and leasing and criticises long rental contracts. This is a competitor's marketing position.
Subscription that spreads the heat pump cost over monthly repayments; customers typically choose to pay back over 10 years.

EU-funded pilots of a subscription model for rented commercial and public buildings, aimed at the landlord-tenant split incentive. The project describes itself as laying foundations, not as having completed results.

name: Tenant electricity (Mieterstrom)
summary: A landlord or contractor installs rooftop PV on an apartment building and sells the power directly to tenants, who still get a grid supply for the rest.
how_it_makes_money: Sale of on-site solar power to tenants at a price below grid supply, plus a federal tenant electricity surcharge and savings on certain levies and grid charges.

hardware: Metering that separates solar from grid power
regulation: German tenant electricity rules and surcharge
data: Metered production and consumption per tenant

stakeholder_value.provider: Revenue from tenant supply and surcharge
stakeholder_value.other: Landlord gets a use for the roof

what_must_be_true: Building is large enough for the project to break even
Smart metering can separate solar and grid power
Enough tenants sign up
Administrative effort stays low

risks_failure_causes.text: Restrictive legal framework and high transaction costs are the main barrier found in expert interviews
Projects on buildings with fewer than 20 residential units tend not to be profitable (Berlin evaluation)
Developers cannot be sure how many tenants will participate; tenants show inertia in switching
In existing buildings smart meters that separate solar and grid power often cannot be installed or cost too much

cases.note: The scheme has been in place since 2017 yet only about 1 percent of its annual budget had been claimed by 2021, and as of April 2024 only about 9,000 PV systems existed on apartment buildings.
74 PV tenant electricity projects with 12.6 MWp were in operation at the end of 2020.

Went through preliminary insolvency proceedings at the turn of the year; the operating business moved to a new company on 1 January 2026, and the tenant electricity business is being handed over to partners such as Polarstern while it focuses on building modernisation strategies.

name: Shared-savings heating optimisation
summary: A provider installs sensors and optimisation software in a building's heating system at no upfront cost to the owner and is paid a share of the measured heating savings.
how_it_makes_money: Provider receives an agreed share of verified heating-energy savings over a contract term. The customer pays no capital expenditure for hardware or software.

software: Web app for customers and operators
sites_assets: Existing building heating systems (multi-family, mixed-use, commercial)
regulation: Building energy regulation and subsidy rules in the target market (check per country)
financing: Provider carries hardware and roll-out cost until savings pay back
channel: Direct to property owners and managers
data: Ongoing metered consumption and sensor data for savings verification

stakeholder_value.customer: Lower heating cost without upfront investment
stakeholder_value.provider: Recurring revenue tied to delivered savings

what_must_be_true: Savings can be measured credibly against an agreed baseline
Achieved savings are large enough to cover provider cost and still leave the customer a gain
The provider can fund hardware and roll-out until payback
Customer accepts a multi-year contract and data access

risks_failure_causes.text: Disagreement on baseline or weather correction makes savings contestable
Low savings in small or already efficient buildings stretch payback beyond what the provider can finance
Owner pays for the system while tenants benefit from lower bills (or the reverse)

cases.note: Sensor-based heating optimisation piloted in multi-family, mixed and commercial buildings; pilots started at 12-15% heating savings. Savings-share model designed with no customer CAPEX. Market outcome of the model to be confirmed.

sources.title: Author's own product work on the Uponor sensor-based heating optimisation pilots

name: Solar system rental or lease (residential)
summary: A provider installs and owns a home PV system (often with battery) and the homeowner pays a flat monthly rent over a long term with no upfront cost; installation, maintenance and insurance are included.
how_it_makes_money: Flat monthly lease payments over about 20 years; the provider also can benefit from incentives as owner of the system. Contribution margin was reported positive from the start in the early years.

hardware: Wallbox or heat pump as add-ons
partners: Investors and lenders funding the installed base
regulation: Grid connection with more than 800 grid operators, each with its own process
financing: Provider or investors carry the system cost for years; overleverage is a risk
channel: Aggressive digital performance marketing and in-house sales

stakeholder_value.customer: No upfront cost, flat monthly payment, service included
stakeholder_value.provider: Long-term recurring revenue and a lasting customer relationship

what_must_be_true: Cost of capital is low enough to fund the installed base
Customers accept a very long contract
Installers can be hired or trained fast enough
Rent stays attractive compared with buying as module and storage prices fall

risks_failure_causes.text: Competitors criticised the rental pricing; the provider publicly defended it
Some customers find the 20-year term too long
Falling prices for modules, storage and wallboxes put many providers under pressure and push customers to buy instead
Funding many rented systems up front can leave the provider overleveraged if customers do not use as much energy as projected

cases.note: Offers a 20-year PV rental with no upfront payment. Had about 10,000 lease customers in 2021 and was not yet profitable then. Added an option to buy in 2023.
Cut staff from nearly 400 to just under 50 in six months; the new CEO said the model it had run for nearly a decade would never have become profitable.

name: Submetering and billing service for landlords
summary: A provider installs radio meters in every unit, reads them remotely and prepares consumption-based heating and water billing for landlords and property managers.
how_it_makes_money: Service fees for metering devices, remote reading, data validation and billing. Exact fee structures are not in the sources and should be added.

hardware: Wireless meters and heat cost allocators
regulation: Heating cost ordinance and national billing and remote-reading rules

stakeholder_value.customer: Landlord: compliant billing without on-site visits
stakeholder_value.provider: Recurring service revenue with high switching effort for customers

what_must_be_true: Regulation requires consumption-based billing and remote reading
Providers reach high remote-reading rates
Landlords stay with their provider

risks_failure_causes.text: The Bundeskartellamt examined the market, which is dominated by a few large players
Customers report misread radio meters and weak support when billing is wrong

cases.note: According to the Bundeskartellamt the two share 50 to 60 percent of the German market. Techem serves more than 13 million apartments and reports about 85 percent wireless reading.

name: Virtual power plant with revenue share for home batteries
summary: An aggregator pools many home batteries (and other flexible devices) into one controllable resource, sells grid services and market products, and shares part of the proceeds with owners.
how_it_makes_money: Revenue from grid services and energy trading, minus the share paid to asset owners and platform costs; the hardware seller can also earn on the battery sale or an electricity contract.

hardware: Home batteries or other flexible assets with remote control
sites_assets: Thousands of distributed assets in customer homes
partners: Trading partner or market access provider
regulation: Prequalification for balancing and reserve markets
financing: Hardware financed by customer, provider or a bundled contract
channel: Bundled with battery sale and electricity contract

stakeholder_value.customer: Share of VPP proceeds, often via an electricity contract

what_must_be_true: Enough assets are pooled to qualify for market products
Market prices leave a margin after the owner share and platform cost
Customers keep their devices online and allow remote control
Rules allow small assets to participate

risks_failure_causes.text: Per-household revenue figures in public sources are small and vary widely, from tens to a few hundred euros per year
Revenue depends on market prices and product rules that can change
Requires reliable internet connection and compatible hardware
The pioneer aggregator sonnen filed for insolvency in October 2026, two months after Shell sold it; services for customers continue

cases.note: Launched SonnenFlat in 2019 sharing VPP proceeds with owners. By 2023 its VPP had 250 MWh with a target of 1 GWh in the following years, providing frequency containment reserve and exchange trading.
Sonnen handles the connection of storage units while marketing and activation of reserve are done through Next Kraftwerke.

Sold by Shell to investor TIVEN in August 2026 and filed for insolvency about two months later, as reported by Handelsblatt via energy-storage.news. Cost cuts did not reach targets. The VPP business of the company was an early mover and customer services continue. The cause is not stated beyond that.
